content:
When I proposed the integrated explicit analytic number theory network structure last year, I was basing my model on existing collaborative, mostly human-generated formalization projects (PNT, Carleson, etc.) in which we tried to maintain a coherent blueprint with reusable code to assist human formalizers (who might receive some modest assistance from 2025-level AI tools) to fill in various lemma-level sorries, in one large common repository.

However, in August 2026 we are now in an era where entire papers can in principle be autoformalized without regards to any carefully curated common base library, using extremely large, non-human-readable formalizations that take a non-trivial amount of time to typecheck. Already many of the papers partially formalized by the existing IEANTN contain such code, but I do not see this system scaling out to a larger range of papers than we are currently targeting.

I am therefore thinking of radically rethinking the IEANTN structure, inspired by the "Challenge / Solution" paradigm of Lean comparator that is for instance used by the recently launched Palomar registry (that I am also involved in). In this new structure, the core IEANTN would consist of a network of challenge files (and a bunch of supporting Defs.lean type files that mostly contain definitions rather than theorems). As a first approximation, each challenge file would correspond to a given paper, with the challenge file for paper A being a human-readable Lean file asserting that the main results of paper A would follow from the main results of various papers B, C, D cited in the references to that paper, as well as some purely computational results that may be beyond the ability of Lean to currently certify. (Eventually, these computational results may be spun off into their own separate challenge files; and there may be auxiliary challenge files created in due course that are not directly associated to a given paper in the literature but reflect some sort of "folklore knowledge" in the subject that needs to be recorded somewhere, e.g., basic estimates on the zeta function). Then, we would also aim to create (almost certainly using modern AI autoformalizers) large solution files for each challenge file that verify the claims in that solution file; but these files would be checked once using Comparator and basically not touched afterwards (unless the challenge file needs to update for some reason). In particular, these large solution files would not be part of the core IEANTN build.

I am still trying to think my way through what is the correct way to refactor this project (including whether it should be spun off to a separate repository than PNT+, now that there is less code reuse), and would appreciate any thoughts on this.

I think a natural direction would be to make IEANTN more explicitly domain-specific, centered on analytic number theory and on maintaining the dependency graph between papers, auxiliary results, and computational inputs (I usually like to work with a clear taxonomy). In my view, if the large AI-generated solutions are no longer intended to form a reusable common codebase, then separating IEANTN from PNT+ would also make sense.

I would probably first try to define more precisely what the responsibility of IEANTN should be, and what should instead be handled by the other projects that are emerging around the same workflow, such as Palomar, Tau Ceti, Formal Frontier, Formal Conjectures, and Math-Challenge.

I think there is a real risk of ending up with a collection of loosely connected projects that each rebuild parts of the same infrastructure. My idea would be to make these projects interoperate as much as possible and assign fairly clear responsibilities to each of them, so that challenge formats, verification, registries, reusable libraries, and domain-specific dependency graphs are not independently reimplemented several times.

Given what AxiomMath did for bounded gap, and what they claimed to be "reusable" for other formalization projects, I couldn't help but think that they could have done the same (especially the beautiful blueprint) for IEANTN. How were these things decided? Could they have better coordinated this? Of course there's big money involved.

Given the current repo size and build time I think that moving the IEANTN things into different repo(s) would be a good idea. PNT could just keep the core PNT result and variants. Perhaps anything which could possibly be upstreamed to Mathlib should stay in PNT.

I am now in the process of building (with heavy AI assistance) a new repository for IEANTN: https://github.com/teorth/IEANTN . It is still incomplete and not yet ready to create issues and accept PRs, but hopefully this will be the case in a week or so.

The structure is now this: IEANTN consists of a compact, human readable core network of "nodes" built around a small "vocabulary", together with much longer, and mostly non-human-readable "solutions" (or other justification) attached to nodes, though currently for most nodes the justification given is "citation to literature" rather than "Lean solution available". For a preliminary glimpse of what the network looks like, see https://github.com/teorth/IEANTN/blob/main/GRAPH.md . The design principle is to make refactoring as easy as possible, through local manipulation of nodes rather than a giant refactor of the entire codebase. Also, the lengthy Lean solutions for each node are kept out of the main CI so that we no longer need over an hour to pass CI.

"Vocabulary" is a collection of short Lean files defining key concepts, such as what a zero-free region of the Riemann zeta function is. It consists almost entirely of definitions, with no actual theorems except what is necessary to form the definitions.

A "node", as a first approximation, corresponds to a published paper, although the intent is to refactor the network over time so that nodes may start drifting from perfect alignment with the results in the literature. A node versioning system is in place to anticipate this: for instance, the FKS2 paper currently has one node FKS2.v1 that is faithful to the paper (modulo typo corrections etc.), but I anticipate later variants FKS2.v2, FKS2.v3, etc. that state the results differently from the original paper.

Each node contains a conclusions file stating (but not proving) their main results in Lean as Props, as well as some metadata recording the dependences of each conclusion (a conclusion from paper X may require importing a conclusion from a prior paper Y, for instance). For instance, here is the FKS2.v1 conclusion file, with the associated formalization.yaml recording the dependencies and other metadata; both are summarized in this auto-generated human-readable summary page. The conclusions can be justified either by appeal to literature, a numerical computation not formalized in Lean, a Lean solution file (checked by comparator), or some other status (partial solution, folklore claim, etc.). This is all summarized in the network graph one can see here.

Currently my focus is on creating all the nodes that are recursively upstream of FKS2, all the way back to Rosser and Schoenfeld; the PNT+ version of the project had manually traced dependencies one or two steps, but with an agentic workflow it now looks very feasible to get the full node network for this generated soon. After that I plan to add in nodes for the other papers already partly formalized in the current network, and begin the porting process (right now I have only ported the proofs from the LCM subproject as a test).

Interestingly, this is very similar to the approach I used for my Lehmer formalization, starting from a complete proof in a standard mathematical paper. I created, at the beginning of the Lean files, a small standardized metadata layer identifying the mathematical role of the file and its place in the proof architecture, with a consistent nomenclature and explicit dependencies that could be used to reconstruct the global DAG automatically.

My goal was to make the entire proof structure inspectable at a glance in a single dependency graph using Graphviz. The Lean files contained the formal content, while the graph gave a referee a compact structural view of the argument, so that one could quickly check whether the decomposition was complete, and the dependency structure was coherent, where the trusted inputs were, and which parts had actually been formally verified. The graph was therefore intended as a proof-audit layer, not merely as documentation.

That feels quite close to the new IEANTN design. The question I am curious about is whether you eventually want this graph to remain paper-local, or whether you would like to normalize the mathematical entities and claims globally across analytic number theory.

I think this becomes especially important if IEANTN is eventually meant to scale beyond target-driven closures around individual papers. Local decomposition works very well for something like FKS2, but after hundreds or thousands of papers the difficult problem may become global normalization rather than extraction itself. Ideally, new papers would reuse already existing mathematical entities and claims wherever possible instead of creating another locally phrased version of the same object or estimate.

If you ever want to explore that direction, I would be happy to contribute. I actually wrote a protocol for this kind of scaling problem, originally for agentic systems, but I think it applies very naturally here.

The idea is to keep a stable taxonomy and ontology with canonical entities, claims, and typed relations, so that each new paper extends a shared reasoning graph rather than creating another partially independent local representation.

This could allow IEANTN nodes to remain the provenance and formal-justification layer while the underlying mathematical graph becomes increasingly reusable and paper-independent. I would be interested in adapting the protocol to a reasoning graph for number theory if that direction is useful.

One option could also be to turn these challenges into some Tau Ceti roadmap(s) for analytic number theory. That way the "solutions" then become code that is much more reusable than what normally comes from targeted autoformalisation projects. It also has the added benefit that you can get others to throw tokens at the project.

At the scale I am envisaging right now (dozens of papers, rather than thousands) I am trying to solve these problems using "bridges", which are small pieces of Lean code that show that the conclusions of node X follow from the conclusions of nodes Y and Z (say), as well as "helper nodes" which contain some API connecting different variants of the same definitional concept.

For instance, in doing the recursive traceback of FKS2, I (or more precisely my agent) discovered that the classical zero-free region {σ+it:t≥t0,σ≥1−1Rlog⁡t} \{ \sigma+it : t \geq t_0, \sigma \geq 1 - \frac{1}{R \log t} \}{σ+it:t≥t0​,σ≥1−Rlogt1​} involves not just the parameter R but also a cutoff t₀ which is chosen slightly differently in different papers (values such as 2, 3, or 21 are used in the literature). Since the low-lying zeroes of zeta are so well understood, it is not difficult to pass from one choice of t₀to another in practice, but this requires some helper API which I formalized in a node https://github.com/teorth/IEANTN/blob/main/docs/nodes/ZeroFreeHeight-v1.md .

An example of a bridge is https://github.com/teorth/IEANTN/blob/main/IEANTN/Bridges/Platt/P2017ToWedeniwski.lean , which records the obvious fact that the numerical RH verification claimed by Wedeniwski is a consequence of the larger numerical RH verification claimed by Platt, allowing any formalized literature claim that previously relied on Wedeniwski to also have an alternate justification using the result of Platt instead.

It's possible that past a certain point, the method of adding bridges and helper API will not scale, but thus far it seems that my agent can cope with it, and in this modern agentic era it seems that refactoring IEANTN again to a version 3.0 that is even more scaleable is not as insanely infeasible as it might have been if we had to do it all by hand.

I come from a point of view where I have not worked without proof assistants in Lean, so I might hold some different viewpoints than most here.

I believe it is incredibly important to have clear theorem-handles which can be brought and used in other projects. I like the idea of being able to efficiently work in props and leave out large solution files from constant builds

My concern is that the graph composition of results, and the difference between an unconditional Lean theorem and a graph-justified conclusion, moves outside the Lean environment. Essentially, I am worried this architecture could allow statements to exist in a dependency graph without there ultimately being an actual kernal typechecked Lean proof of the final result. Then, the verification of the system as a whole moves from Lean to again manual (or perhaps agentic) work, which is exactly what we're trying to avoid?

I currently see the issue of large codebases in lean similar to any large code base with many tests and builds. Perhaps it is better to look into proper caching of results, rather than continuously building the results each and every time. .olean files already do this but newer lean versions always make for hassles, and refactoring often becomes messy from what I've noticed.

The problem is that trusted solutions cannot easily be trusted on the next run, we keep building and verifying the same theorems on each build. If a large solution has already been checked, ideally I would like downstream projects to be able to import its theorem handles without rebuilding the underlying source constantly, while still keeping the result inside Lean's normal trust. Perhaps there is a better method to make this transitive across versions?
Maybe this is a failure on my part to see why this keeps being necessary, or what limitation exists such that this is not being solved already?

I also still believe readable code is very important to the development of efficient proofs, though I hold the belief that models will in the coming months improve significantly in this regard anyhow. The most important thing is still to expose useful and important theorems most easily to further develop on, and their proofs can also guide further proofs and methods.

This would ensure that important work can still be included into mathlib, and can be properly reused and learned from.

Additionally, although I like the idea of trusting papers as they are, I believe that they can be used as props but should not be seen as actually being solved already. How is this different than current methods of proving conditional statements which is already being done in lean? I still highly prefer to trust lean in this case, and not imports from informal papers. As an example, see the recent complex structure on S_6 which would then be able to take the CDP paper as a prop/conditional, which wouldn't have worked.

In addition, such dependency graphs work amazingly for smaller projects, but if adopted as an architecture, when the foundations of the graph are not completely backed by lean, one can later find errors which lean would have already caught for you. Lean is great because if the final theorem is correct and unconditional, you can get as close to a certification that it is true as possible right now. Moving to a propositional based or perhaps a informal-based method would lose this. Currently, a propositional proof can be identified easily as one only has to certify the final shown theorem, and if built without errors, one can then trust the proof. In the proposed architecture, such "simple" verifications will be lost.

However, I do believe organizing around a dependency graph or the like would be useful. Is there perhaps a better way to certify some lean statements more cleanly such that we can circumvent the current limitations better than trusting a somewhat uncheck dependency graph?
At the global level, if the final result is represented through a chain of independently justified nodes rather than a composed Lean proof, how different is this to a highly structured and machine-audited blueprint already?

Please let me know if I misunderstood some point, but the certification of the whole graph makes lean powerful for me, and without this certification, in what way would we improve on informal maths? If we can significantly advance on being able to import or trust/reuse already proven theorems without the long build times or hoarding huge dependencies, that would be a greater contribution in my eyes.

I view certification as a continuum; results are not simply in a binary state of "formally certified" or "completely uncertified", but can exist in an intermediate state, in which formal reductions are available to some previous results, which can give multiple options regarding how to trust any given result. I intend the network to become multiply connected over time, so that individual results can have multiple justifications.

For the IEANTN in particular, full Lean justification of every step is likely infeasible due to the presence of extremely large computational inputs, such as numerical verification of the Riemann hypothesis up to a given height. But such verifications can be performed independently by several groups, each of which can be tracked by a node on the IEANTN, and so again one can improve the relative confidence in a result relying on such a verification using the graph. Or one can simply accept a conditional result that the conclusion of a given paper is true assuming that the outcome of certain specific numerical calculations are trusted.

I have not yet performed a mathlib bump on the new IEANTN, but I view the issues caused by some certifications of lengthy proofs becoming stale due to mathlib drift to be an acceptable one. The graph records the mathlib version at which any given certification took place, and should flag (using suitable color coding, such as an amber traffic light emoji) if a certification is stale and needs to be updated to the most current Mathlib version supported by the IEANTN. But I believe that this process can be done independently of building out the rest of the network, and only slightly degrades the ability to trust any given result.

Currently I don't plan to generate an end-to-end Lean certificate for any result that does manage to get formalized through a chain of intermediate conditional verifications, but this looks very feasible (especially to modern agents). In the Equational Theories project we also discussed the possibility of an end-to-end Lean certificate of the final implication graph, but in the end we were content with only formalizing a generating set of edges and relying on Python scripts to certify all the 22 million or so other edges as a consequence.

My main objective with the IEANTN is to at least eliminate the possibility of mundane errors (such as sign errors) within the literature and move the trust boundary to very explicit large computations that can be independently replicated; and then also to convert these papers into a more "pipeline" form that can dynamically convert input estimates into output estimates. My dream is to eventually make an IEANTN "spreadsheet" in which one can input, for instance, all the computational work on RH done up to 2010, and automatically generate the best prime number theorems that can be formally derived from that work as a consequence. Such a generated list may not be 100% Lean certified as a single proof, but I think it can be useful even below this 100% certification standard, if we can use formalization eradicate the type of fragile error that would otherwise destroy a lengthy chain of computational evaluation of various numerical constants.

This indeed sounds exciting, I think I am mostly convinced, though I still hope to work with final Lean certified theorems without such propositions if possible, I can believe such a node based system can improve over time more reliably than current monorepos.

There is still some engineering I feel can be improved upon in regard to Challenges and Solutions, to me it sounds a bit sloppy, but it's more of an arbitrary opinion. Agents will be able to enforce it, and we can use the results further.

A win-win regardless.

After building on anthropics/zeta-23-lean, we got a bound on the number of zeta's simple zeros.

The theorem is parameterised for n, and the proof needs one finite inequality that Lean doesn't check. That's an assumption in the statement.

At n=3 and n=4 , it was proved in Lean, so that dropped the assumption. At n=7 and n=8 nobody has proved it, so it's still assumed there.

Same theorem, but the n cases are certified differently. How would that get recorded?

Terence Tao said:

I view certification as a continuum; results are not simply in a binary state of "formally certified" or "completely uncertified", but can exist in an intermediate state, in which formal reductions are available to some previous results, which can give multiple options regarding how to trust any given result.

That makes a lot of sense. And, from my perspective, the higher the complexity, the less binary the certification becomes, as the margin for uncertainty inevitably grows...

An update: I have managed to certify the head node of FKS2, which is green at https://github.com/teorth/IEANTN/blob/main/GRAPH.md . What this means is that we now have a Lean certified proof that the conclusions of FKS2 follow from the conclusions of the nodes flowing into that node. There are a bunch of other blue nodes downstream for which it is feasible to perform a similar certification (possibly after some refactoring of the node graph), at which point FKS2 will be completely derived from computational nodes (in yellow) which would be infeasible to check in Lean but are straightforward to replicate by traditional computation. I'll start issuing tasks to do this (with a recommendation to use AI agents to navigate the specific format required for the IEANTN repository) shortly.

I've now created a separate project board for IEANTN: https://github.com/teorth/IEANTN . The porting process is still underway, and legacy IEANTN issues on the PNT+ board will still be processed for now, but the plan is to transition out of the PNT+ repository and move fully on to the IEANTN repository. In particular once the port is complete, IEANTN code can be removed from the PNT+ repository which should significantly improve build times in PNT+. (For IEANTN build times are much better by design, because the solutions files are not part of the core build and are verified separately in a very occasional manner by a comparator run.)
